lesson.title: Straight Lines From Curves: Building a Bode Magnitude Plot
lesson.summary: A Bode magnitude plot graphs decibel magnitude against a logarithmic frequency axis, letting an engineer sketch a filter's entire response as two straight line asymptotes that meet at the corner frequency.
lesson.body:
Magnitude Response already established the decibel values for the RC low pass filter at several frequencies, and Decade defines a tenfold change in frequency as the natural unit for the horizontal axis of these plots. A Bode Magnitude Plot puts both ideas together: it graphs 20 log10(|H(jw)|) in decibels on the vertical axis against frequency on a logarithmic horizontal axis, measured in decades. The payoff for using a log frequency axis is that a first order filter's magnitude response becomes, to a very good approximation, two straight line segments meeting at a corner.

Recall the values already computed for R = 1000 ohms, C = 1 microfarad, corner frequency wc = 1000 rad/s: -0.043 dB at w = 100 rad/s, -3.010 dB at w = 1000 rad/s, and -20.043 dB at w = 10000 rad/s. The straight line asymptotic approximation used for hand sketching says the magnitude stays flat at 0 dB for all frequencies below wc, then falls in a straight line at a rate of -20 dB per decade for all frequencies above wc. Check this against the numbers just listed: from w = 1000 to w = 10000 is exactly one decade, and the asymptote predicts a drop of 20 dB, landing at -20 dB, while the true computed value is -20.043 dB, an error of only 0.043 dB.

Extend the check one more decade to see the pattern hold. At w = 100000 rad/s, two decades above the corner, wRC = 100, so |H| = 1/square root of (1 + 100 squared) = 1/square root of 10001 = 1/100.005 = 0.0099995, and the magnitude in decibels is 20 log10(0.0099995) = 20 times (-2.00002) = -40.0004 dB. The straight line asymptote, falling at -20 dB per decade for two decades past 0 dB, predicts exactly -40 dB. The true value of -40.0004 dB matches to within four ten thousandths of a decibel, confirming that far from the corner the straight line approximation becomes essentially exact.

The only place the asymptote and the true curve disagree by a meaningful amount is right at the corner frequency itself, where the flat line and the falling line meet at 0 dB in the idealized sketch but the true response has already dropped to -3.010 dB, as shown in Magnitude Response. This 3 dB gap at the corner is a well known, fixed correction that anyone sketching a Bode magnitude plot by hand simply remembers and applies, rounding the sharp corner of the asymptote into a smooth dip at exactly that one point.

This is why the Bode magnitude plot is such a powerful design tool: an engineer can sketch the entire shape of a filter's frequency response, flat region, corner frequency, and roll off slope, using nothing but two straight lines and one remembered correction, without ever touching a calculator, and the numeric verification above shows that sketch is accurate to a fraction of a decibel everywhere except within about half a decade of the corner frequency on either side.
